commonMistakes: Torso leaning far forward over the front thigh
Pushing off the back foot instead of driving through the front leg
cues: Tall torso, ribs stacked over hips
Front knee tracks over the middle of your foot
Drive through the whole front foot to stand
instructions: Take a long staggered stance, one foot forward and one back, torso tall and core braced. Hold onto a wall or rack for balance if needed.
Lower straight down until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor and your back knee hovers just above the ground.
Keep most of your weight on the front leg; the back leg is a kickstand, not a driver.
Drive through your front foot to stand. Complete all reps on one side before switching.
longevityNotes: Single-leg strength is balance, and balance is independence: falls are the leading cause of injury in older adults, and the split squat trains the exact pattern — one leg loaded, body stable — that keeps you on your feet. It also evens out left-right strength differences that bilateral squats hide. Start bodyweight, hold a wall, and earn your depth; the goal is a controlled single-leg squat you can still do at 75, not a wobbly weighted one today.
name: Split Squat

progression.loadingGuidance: Add dumbbells when you can do 3 sets of 10 per leg with a 2-second pause at the bottom, no balance assist.
progression.regressTo: Assisted split squat holding a doorframe or TRX

safetyNotes: If you have acute knee pain, shorten the range to your pain-free zone and keep the front knee behind the toes initially. Use balance support freely — a fall during the exercise defeats its purpose.
